meta.titre: Work, energy and power: calculations, efficiency and energy sources
meta.sous_theme: work, energy conservation, power and efficiency

sections.contenu_markdown: A builder in Douala carries bags of cement up a ladder to a roof, a farmer in Foumbot pumps water to his vegetable garden, and a family in Maroua buys a solar panel to charge phones. Each of these uses energy, does work at a certain rate and wastes some of the energy as heat. Work, energy and power are the vocabulary of every physics problem about machines and fuel, and the GCE asks for them in nearly every paper, from naming the stored energy in a battery to calculating the efficiency of a pump.

items: The weight of an object is its mass multiplied by $g$, with $g=10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$.
Force is measured in newtons and distance in metres.
Time is measured in seconds and 1 minute is 60 seconds.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Work.** Work is done when a force moves an object in the direction of the force:

$$W=F\times d\qquad(\text{joule, J})$$

$F$ is the force in newtons and $d$ the distance moved **in the direction of the force** in metres. When an object is lifted at steady speed, the force is its weight $mg$, so the work is $mgh$. Holding a heavy load without moving it does no work in the physics sense.

**Energy** is the ability to do work, also measured in joules. Two mechanical forms:

- **Gravitational potential energy** (height): $E_p=mgh$
- **Kinetic energy** (movement): $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$

**Conservation of energy.** Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it changes from one form to another. Falling without friction, potential energy turns into kinetic energy: $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$. The energy transferred is the same as the work done.

**Power** is the rate of doing work or transferring energy:

$$P=\frac{W}{t}=\frac{E}{t}\qquad(\text{watt, W})$$

$1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$. Electrical power is also $P=VI$.

**Efficiency.** No machine turns all its input energy into useful output. Some is wasted, mostly as heat.

$$\text{efficiency}=\frac{\text{useful energy (or power) output}}{\text{total energy (or power) input}}\times100\,\%$$

Efficiency is always less than $100\,\%$.

**Forms of energy:** chemical (food, fuels, batteries), kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, electrical, light, sound, nuclear.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to classify energy sources or to name one advantage or disadvantage.
variantes.contenu_markdown: **Renewable** sources are replaced as fast as we use them: solar, wind, hydroelectric (moving water), tidal, geothermal and biomass (wood, biogas). **Non-renewable** sources will run out: coal, oil, natural gas and nuclear fuel (uranium). Hydroelectric power, as at the Edea and Song Loulou dams in Cameroon, uses the potential energy of water stored high up: potential energy $\to$ kinetic energy $\to$ electrical energy. Fuels also add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere, while solar and wind do not.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When an object falls, is thrown up or swings and you must find its speed or height.
variantes.contenu_markdown: If friction is ignored, the potential energy lost equals the kinetic energy gained: $mgh=\tfrac12mv^2$, so $v=\sqrt{2gh}$ (mass cancels). Doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by $4$, since $E_k\propto v^2$. If energy is wasted (air resistance, sound), the kinetic energy at the bottom is less than $mgh$ and the difference is the energy transferred as heat to the surroundings.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A crane at a building site in Douala lifts a concrete block of mass $200\ \mathrm{kg}$ through a height of $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ at steady speed in $15\ \mathrm{s}$. The electric motor of the crane takes in energy at a rate of $1000\ \mathrm{W}$. Take $g=10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$.

(a) Calculate the work done on the block.

(b) Calculate the useful power output of the crane.

(c) Calculate the efficiency of the crane and say what happens to the wasted energy.

etapes.action: Find the force needed to lift at steady speed.
etapes.justification: At steady speed the lifting force equals the weight of the block.
The force and the movement are both vertical, so use $W=Fd$.
Power is work divided by time.
Compare the useful power output with the power input.
The difference between input and useful output is wasted.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $1000-800=200\ \mathrm{W}$, so $200\ \mathrm{J}$ is wasted every second as heat and sound in the motor, cables and pulleys.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** $12\,000\ \mathrm{J}$. **(b)** $800\ \mathrm{W}$. **(c)** Efficiency $=80\,\%$; the remaining $20\,\%$ is wasted as heat and sound.

items.erreur_markdown: Work done lifting a $200\ \mathrm{kg}$ block through $6\ \mathrm{m}$: $W=200\times6=1200\ \mathrm{J}$
items.pourquoi_faux: The force in $W=Fd$ must be in newtons. A mass of $200\ \mathrm{kg}$ has a weight of $2000\ \mathrm{N}$, not $200\ \mathrm{N}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “A man holding a heavy sack above his head for one hour does a lot of work.”
items.pourquoi_faux: In physics, work needs movement in the direction of the force. If the sack does not move, $d=0$, so $W=0$ (the man gets tired, but no work is done on the sack).
items.correction_markdown: Work is done only when the force moves its point of application.

items.erreur_markdown: “If the speed of a car doubles, its kinetic energy doubles.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Kinetic energy depends on $v^2$. Doubling $v$ makes $v^2$ four times as large.
items.correction_markdown: $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$: doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by $4$.

items.pourquoi_faux: The fraction is upside down. Output must be divided by input and a real machine cannot be more than $100\,\%$ efficient.

items.erreur_markdown: “Power and energy are the same thing, so a 60 W lamp uses 60 J.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Power is the energy used per second. A $60\ \mathrm{W}$ lamp uses $60\ \mathrm{J}$ **every second**.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained by a $3.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ bag of rice lifted onto a shelf $4.0\ \mathrm{m}$ high. ($g=10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$)

(b) Calculate the kinetic energy of a $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ ball moving at $6.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

An electric pump lifts $600\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water through a height of $5.0\ \mathrm{m}$ every minute. The pump takes in electrical power of $800\ \mathrm{W}$. ($g=10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$)

(a) Calculate the work done on the water each minute.

(b) Calculate the useful power output.

(c) Calculate the efficiency of the pump.

A ball of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ is dropped from a height of $20\ \mathrm{m}$ onto hard ground. ($g=10\ \mathrm{N\,kg^{-1}}$)

(a) Calculate its potential energy before it is dropped.

(b) Ignoring air resistance, calculate its speed just before it hits the ground.

(c) The ball rebounds to a height of $12.5\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate the energy lost in the bounce and the percentage of the original energy that is lost.

(d) Name two forms of energy into which the lost energy is changed.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $E_p=mgh=0.50\times10\times20=$ **$100\ \mathrm{J}$**.

(b) All of this becomes kinetic energy: $\tfrac12mv^2=100$, so $v^2=\dfrac{2\times100}{0.50}=400$ and $v=$ **$20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

(c) Energy at the top of the rebound $=0.50\times10\times12.5=62.5\ \mathrm{J}$. Energy lost $=100-62.5=$ **$37.5\ \mathrm{J}$**, which is $\dfrac{37.5}{100}\times100\,\%=$ **$37.5\,\%$**.

(d) Heat (the ball and ground warm up) and sound.

items_markdown: Work $W=Fd$ (joules) with the distance in the direction of the force; lifting a mass gives $W=mgh$.
Potential energy $E_p=mgh$ and kinetic energy $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$; doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.
Energy is conserved: it changes form (for example $E_p\to E_k$) but is never created or destroyed.
Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\times100\,\%$ is always less than $100\,\%$; the rest is wasted as heat.
Renewable sources: solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, biomass. Non-renewable: coal, oil, gas, nuclear fuel. A car battery stores chemical energy.
